# What was the ONS CIS worth?

Idea note, Aug 2026.
Separate from a related PhD project, but shares its ascertainment machinery.

## Question

CIS was expensive and is gone.
If something similar happens again, the question will be whether to rebuild it, at what size, and how often to run it.

Better to avoid asking "was it worth it", which needs a decision model and a willingness-to-pay threshold we do not have.
Ask instead: how much of what CIS told us was recoverable without it, and at what sampling intensity?

Ex-post, empirical, answerable.
Not ex-ante VOI in the health-economic sense, and should be labelled as such.

## Bridge: case ascertainment

CIS and case data differ by ascertainment.
So `a(t) = cases(t) / CIS infections(t)` is the exact quantity CIS bought.

Nouvellet reference: one covariate, one link function, no elaborate structure.

- `a(t) ~ test positivity` --- Chiu and Ndeffo-Mbah 2021, geometric mean of cases and positivity approximates prevalence.
- `a(t) ~ testing eligibility policy` --- OxCGRT H2, free and available for every country.

Both computable with no survey at all.

## Three counterfactuals

1. No CIS.
   Reconstruct infections from cases and positivity alone.
   How wrong, and wrong where?
2. CIS as periodic calibration.
   Fit the ascertainment link on a short CIS window, apply prospectively, never refit.
   How long does a calibration last before it decays?
3. CIS at reduced intensity.
   Retrospectively thin the survey --- monthly instead of weekly, a fraction of the sample --- and recompute.
   Error against survey cost.

Third is the real output: a design curve rather than a verdict.

## The interesting bit

CIS value is not constant over time.
It should be highest when ascertainment is moving fastest (capacity ramp in spring, demand crunch in September) and near zero when ascertainment is stable, because a stable `a` is recoverable from anything.

Implication: a fixed-frequency survey is inefficient.
Run it hard when the ascertainment mapping is drifting, and let it idle when it is not.
Adaptive sampling triggered by divergence between free proxies.

That is a design recommendation with a real generalisation beyond England, and it is the part worth building the analysis around.

## Relation to other work

Shares machinery with a related PhD project, which asks a different question.
This owns the survey-design side --- how much randomised sampling do you actually need.

## To check

- CIS cost.
- Whether CIS microdata (participant swab, collection date) are accessible, or only modelled outputs.
  Determines whether thinning is honest or simulated.
- Whether inc2prev can be refit on thinned data without falling over.
- Existing evaluations of CIS.
  Someone at ONS or UKHSA may have done a version of this already.
- Whether REACT gives a second randomised series to cross-check against, which would strengthen counterfactual 1 considerably.

## Related

- [cis-ascertainment](cis-ascertainment.qmd) --- CIS asked participants about tests taken outside the study, so ascertainment can be measured on people rather than reconstructed from a ratio. Changes how counterfactuals 1 and 2 would be built.
- `ensemble-marginal-value` (kath-a-log #26) --- informational value as reduction in forecast variance against a partial-information baseline.
  The Baur and Orazem setup is close to counterfactual 1 in spirit.
